result.topic_en: Euler reduces the eclipse equation to small-angle series, solves for the time t at which the Moon's orbital longitude equals the shadow's ecliptic longitude relative to mid-eclipse, and gives the resulting longitudes of shadow and Moon.
result.transcription:
At cum sit
$\cos(2x+(m+n+2k)(h-t)'') = \cos 2x \cos(m+n+2k)(h-t)'' - \sin 2x \sin(m+n+2k)(h-t)''$
$\cos(2x-(m+n+2k)t'') = \cos 2x \cos(m+n+2k)t'' + \sin 2x \sin(m+n+2k)t''$
quo calculus ad sinus et cosinus angulorum satis parvorum reducitur: qui anguli cum dentur in secundis, ii multiplicentur per numerum $g = 0,0000048481$, seu $lg = 4,6855749$, ut reducantur[?] ad partes radii, qui ponitur $=1$; eritque sinibus et cosinibus horum angulorum per series convergentes expressis
$(1+\cos\varrho)\left(1-\tfrac{1}{2}ggtt(n-m)^2 - 1 + \tfrac{1}{2}gg(h-t)^2(n-m)^2\right) =$
$(1-\cos\varrho)\left\{\begin{array}{l} +\cos 2x\left(1-\tfrac{1}{2}gg(h-t)^2(m+n+2k)^2\right) - \sin 2x\left(g(h-t)(m+n+2k)\right) \\ -\cos 2x\left(1-\tfrac{1}{2}ggtt(m+n+2k)^2\right) - \sin 2x \cdot gt(m+n+2k) \end{array}\right.$
$= (1-\cos\varrho)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}gg(m+n+2k)^2(2ht-hh)\cos 2x - gh(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\right)$
§ 10. Hac ergo aequatione debite tractata reperiemus
$(1+\cos\varrho)\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}gg(n-m)^2(hh-2ht) = (1-\cos\varrho)\cdot gh(m+n+2k)\left(\tfrac{1}{2}g(m+n+2k)(2t-h)\cos 2x - \sin 2x\right)$
seu $g(h-2t)(n-m)^2 = \mathrm{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho\,(m+n+2k)\left(g(m+n+2k)(2t-h)\cos 2x - 2\sin 2x\right)$
vel hoc modo
$\left.\begin{array}{l} gh(n-m)^2 + gh(m+n+2k)^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho \\ + 2(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho \end{array}\right\} = 2gt(n-m)^2 + 2gt(m+n+2k)^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$
Hinc ergo eruetur
$2t-h = \frac{2(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(m+n+2k)^2\cos 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho + g(n-m)^2}$
et ob $\mathrm{tang}^2\tfrac{1}{2}\varrho$ tantopere parvum, erit
$t = \tfrac{1}{2}h + \frac{(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(n-m)^2} - \frac{(m+n+2k)^3\sin 2x\cos 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^4\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(n-m)^4}$
ubi ultimus terminus ob summam parvitatem facile negligitur.
§ 11. In hac aequatione terminus $\tfrac{1}{2}h$ designat medium totius eclipsis momentum, quod ex observationibus vel initii et finis eclipsis, vel immersionis et emersionis facile concluditur. Momentum ergo, quo longitudo lunae in orbita et longitudo umbrae in ecliptica inter se fiunt aequales, post medium eclipsis incidit elapsis horis $\frac{(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(n-m)^2}$. Quamobrem si pro eclipsis momento medio computemus et longitudinem lunae in orbita, quae sit $=L$, et longitudinem umbrae seu oppositionem solis, quae sit $=U$, ex motu horario erit illo altero momento, quo utraque longitudo fit aequalis
longitudo umbrae $= U + \frac{m(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(n-m)^2}$
longitudo lunae $= L + \frac{n(m+n+2k)\sin 2x\,\mathrm{tang}^2\frac{1}{2}\varrho}{g(n-m)^2}$

items.english: where the last term, because of its extreme smallness, is easily neglected.

items.english: In this equation the term ½h denotes the middle moment of the whole eclipse, which is easily inferred from observations either of the beginning and end of the eclipse, or of the immersion and emersion.
